extra.message: The JWT SECRET_KEY uses a hardcoded fallback value 'change-me-in-production-local-dev-only' when the SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. This well-known default allows any attacker to forge arbitrary JWT tokens and impersonate any user, including admins.

The JWT SECRET_KEY defaults to 'change-me-in-production-local-dev-only' if not set via environment variable. This weak default key could allow attackers to forge valid JWT tokens and impersonate any user, including admins.

The JWT algorithm is read from the `ALGORITHM` environment variable with no validation. This could be set to 'none' (disabling signature verification) or other weak algorithms. Combined with the permissive default, this creates a risk of JWT algorithm confusion attacks.
The default DATABASE_URL contains plaintext credentials 'postgres:postgres' embedded directly in the connection string as the fallback value.

The `DATABASE_URL` environment variable has a default value of `postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/supportdesk` which contains hardcoded credentials (`postgres:postgres`). If the env var is not configured, the application connects to a database with widely known default credentials.

The application has no CSRF protection middleware. The auth system falls back to reading the JWT from a cookie (get_current_user), and while SameSite=Lax provides partial mitigation, CSRF protection should be explicitly implemented for defense-in-depth.

The `/api/auth/login` endpoint has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism. An attacker can attempt unlimited password guesses against any user account, enabling credential brute-forcing and password spraying attacks.

The login endpoint sets the access_token as an HTTP-only cookie (line 82), and the auth.py get_current_user function (line 59) accepts the token from cookies as a fallback. However, state-changing POST endpoints (create_ticket, create_reply, etc.) accept this cookie-based authentication without CSRF protection. A victim logged into the application could be tricked into visiting a malicious site that submits cross-origin requests that execute state changes.
The session cookie (access_token) is set without the 'secure=True' flag. The cookie will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, making it vulnerable to network interception.
The create_user endpoint returns 'Email already registered' when a duplicate email is provided, allowing an attacker to determine which email addresses are registered in the system.

The update_user endpoint binds all fields from UserUpdate (which includes role, is_active, organization_id) directly to the user model via setattr. While require_admin is enforced on the endpoint, the schema allows these privileged fields to be set from request input, and there is no validation or allowlist checking which specific fields are appropriate for the operation.
The list_organizations endpoint returns ALL organizations with no pagination. With a large number of organizations, this query could consume excessive database and memory resources.

The OrganizationCreate schema includes plan_type and is_active fields which are bound directly via Organization(**org_in.model_dump()). An admin creating an organization can set plan_type to 'enterprise' or is_active to True/False directly from the request, bypassing any business logic around plan assignment or activation workflows.
The list_teams endpoint returns ALL teams with no pagination and uses joinedload on members.

The update_team endpoint uses for-loop setattr to bind all fields from TeamCreate (including is_active) to the team model without restriction. An admin can deactivate a team directly through this endpoint without any additional validation or confirmation.

In the list_tickets endpoint, for support_agent role, the authorization filter is only applied when the agent has teams. If a support_agent has no teams (empty team_ids list), the condition 'if team_ids:' is False, and NO organization or team filter is applied, returning ALL tickets in the system. This bypasses the scoping intended by the authorization model.

In the list_tickets endpoint, support_agent and team_lead roles filter by team but include unassigned tickets (team_id IS NULL) without any organization scoping. This allows an agent from one organization's team to view tickets from other organizations that happen to be unassigned.

The _authorize_ticket function only checks team membership for support_agent when ticket.team_id is set. If ticket.team_id is None (unassigned ticket), the check passes unconditionally, allowing any agent from any organization to view any unassigned ticket.

The create_ticket endpoint sets org_id to current_user.organization_id only for customer_user role (line 420), and sets it to None for all other roles. The check on line 421-422 ('if not org_id') then raises a 400 error for staff users because their organization_id is typically None. This means support agents, team leads, and admins CANNOT create tickets through this endpoint — only customer users can.

The `update_ticket` endpoint uses `require_any` (allowing customer users) and only calls `_authorize_ticket` which checks VIEW-level authorization (whether the user can see the ticket). It does NOT restrict which fields customers can update. The `TicketUpdate` schema includes `assignee_id`, `team_id`, `status`, `priority`, and `category_id` — all fields customers should never be allowed to modify. A customer could set the assignee, change the team, or escalate priority on their own tickets.

The update_ticket endpoint uses require_any (any authenticated user) for authorization and calls _authorize_ticket which only checks READ-level access (org match for customers, team match for agents). After this read-level check, ALL fields from TicketUpdate (including assignee_id, team_id, status, priority, category_id) are bound wholesale to the ticket model via setattr at lines 468-469. A customer_user can modify any field of a ticket within their organization, including reassigning it, changing its status, altering priority, or modifying subject/description.

The `create_note` endpoint uses `require_staff` which correctly excludes customers. However, the `update_note` endpoint at line 539 also uses `require_staff` and checks ownership, which is correct. This finding is NOT about notes — it's about ensuring completeness. Actually verified: these are properly protected.

The file upload endpoint accepts any file type. The mime_type is taken directly from the client-supplied Content-Type header without validation. An attacker could upload malicious files (e.g., executable scripts, HTML with JavaScript) that could be served to other users via the download endpoint.

The file upload endpoint does not validate file size. The entire file content is read into memory with file.file.read() before being written to disk, allowing an attacker to upload arbitrarily large files and cause memory exhaustion or disk filling.

The file upload endpoint does not validate file type or extension. The original filename's extension is extracted and used, allowing upload of .html, .exe, .js, or other potentially dangerous file types. These files are then served via the /uploads static mount.

The upload_attachment endpoint accepts files with any extension (including .html, .exe, .php, .sh) and stores them on disk using the user-supplied extension. Combined with the StaticFiles mount at /uploads (line 1213), uploaded .html files containing JavaScript could be accessed and executed in a browser, leading to stored XSS.

The file upload endpoint at `/api/tickets/{ticket_id}/attachments` does not validate the uploaded file's content or content type. An attacker can upload an HTML file with `Content-Type: text/html`. When downloaded via the download endpoint (line 623), `FileResponse` serves the file inline (Content-Disposition: inline) with the attacker-supplied mime_type, causing the browser to render it as HTML and execute any embedded JavaScript in the application's origin context.

The update_escalation endpoint uses for-loop setattr to bind all fields from EscalationUpdate (including owner_id, status, resolution) directly to the escalation model without validation. A team_lead with access to an escalation can set owner_id to any user ID, arbitrarily assigning ownership of escalations.

The KBArticleCreate schema includes is_internal which is directly passed via **article_in.model_dump(). A staff user creating a KB article can decide whether the article is internal or public by setting this field. While staff can set internal articles, this bypasses any workflow or approval process for marking content as internal.

The KBArticleUpdate schema includes is_internal which is bound via setattr in the update handler. A staff user can change a published article from public to internal (or vice versa) directly, potentially hiding or exposing sensitive content without oversight.
The _trigger_webhook function has a try/except block that silently swallows all exceptions from audit_log, which could hide database errors or other failures in the auditing system.

The import_customers endpoint only checks that the filename ends with '.csv', but does not validate the actual file content or prevent files with embedded path traversal characters. A file named 'malware.csv.exe' or '../../etc/passwd.csv' would pass the check.

All users imported via the /api/import/customers endpoint are created with the same hardcoded default password 'changeme123'. There is no mechanism to force password change on first login, leaving all imported accounts vulnerable to takeover if the default password is known.
The CSV import endpoint creates customer accounts with a hardcoded default password 'changeme123'. All imported customers share the same weak password.

The export_tickets endpoint requires require_staff but does NOT filter tickets by the current user's teams or any access scope. Any staff member (including a support_agent) can export ALL tickets in the system, including those from organizations and teams they don't belong to.

The ticket CSV export writes user-controlled fields (subject, organization name, requester name, assignee name) directly into CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. If these fields start with '=', '+', '-', or '@', they will be interpreted as formulas when opened in Excel, LibreOffice, or Google Sheets.
The export_sla endpoint requires require_staff but does not filter by user access scope. Any staff member can export SLA performance data for ALL tickets across all organizations.

The SLA CSV export writes user-controlled fields (subject, organization name, assignee name) directly into CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. Same pattern as the ticket export.
The dashboard_stats endpoint allows any authenticated user (including customer users) to view global ticket statistics across ALL organizations, revealing sensitive business intelligence.

Uploaded files are mounted as static files at /uploads without any authentication check. While the /api/attachments/{id}/download endpoint has proper authorization, the static mount bypasses all auth — anyone who knows or guesses the UUID filename can access any uploaded file directly.

While the forgot-password endpoint returns a consistent message ('If an account exists, a reset link has been sent'), it still queries the database and creates an audit log entry, potentially leaking existence via timing side-channels or audit log analysis.

The /api/auth/forgot-password endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing unlimited password reset requests. Although the endpoint always returns the same message (mitigating email enumeration), it can still be abused to trigger excessive audit log writes and email sending.

The forgot-password endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to enumerate valid email addresses by observing timing differences or response differences, and to flood users with password reset emails.

The `/api/auth/reset-password` endpoint accepts `email`, `token`, and `new_password` but never verifies the `token` parameter. The comment on line 1238 states 'In production, verify token' but no verification is implemented. Any unauthenticated attacker who knows a user's email can reset their password by providing any arbitrary token value.

The `/api/auth/reset-password` endpoint returns HTTP 404 with 'User not found' if the email doesn't exist, but returns HTTP 200 if it does. This discrepancy allows unauthenticated attackers to determine which email addresses are registered in the system.
The reset-password endpoint has no rate limiting, which combined with the missing token verification (CWE-640) allows unlimited password reset attempts.

The reset_password endpoint accepts a 'token' parameter but never validates it. The comment '# In production, verify token' indicates the verification is not implemented. Anyone who knows a user's email can reset their password.
The reset_password endpoint returns different responses for existing and non-existing users ('User not found' vs success), allowing email enumeration.
The reset-password endpoint returns a 404 error with 'User not found' if the email doesn't exist but returns success (or other error) if it does. This allows account enumeration.

The reset_password endpoint returns different responses depending on whether the email exists in the system: 404 'User not found' for non-existent emails vs (presumably) 200 for existing ones. This allows attackers to enumerate valid user email addresses.

The WebhookConfig model's 'secret' field (Column String(255)) stores the webhook signing secret in plaintext. If the database is compromised, webhook secrets can be read directly, allowing attackers to forge webhook payloads to external services.
The `packet_ref` query parameter is used directly to construct a file path without sanitization. An attacker can include '../' sequences to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.

The user-controlled `packet_ref` parameter is used to construct a file path without validation. An attacker can use path traversal sequences (e.g., `../../etc/cron.d/malicious`) to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem. Request body is written as file content.

The request body is written directly to a file with no size limits or content validation. Combined with the path traversal vulnerability, an attacker could write arbitrarily large files or malicious content (e.g., cron jobs, SSH keys) to the filesystem.

The `delta_value` is parsed from user input as a float with NO bounds validation (no positive check, no min/max). A negative or excessively large value could invert or amplify whatever financial/state-changing operation this delta represents.

The `ticket_agent_file_120` endpoint has no `gate_ref` dependency, meaning it is publicly accessible without any authentication, unlike most other endpoints in this file which require the internal ops token.

The endpoint `/fold/ticket-agent-file-120` has no `Depends(_wrk_gate)` authentication dependency, unlike all other endpoints in this router. It returns sensitive operational memo data including "renewal risk, payment flags, owner contact details".

The `lane` query parameter is passed directly to `RedirectResponse()` without validation. An attacker with the internal ops token can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs, enabling phishing attacks.

User-supplied JSON payload is merged directly into a workset dictionary via `workset.update(payload)`. This allows the user to override security-critical fields like `role`, `approved`, `balance`, and `tier`.

The `workset` dictionary is initialized with secure defaults (`approved: False`, `role: "viewer"`) but then `workset.update(payload)` allows the user to override any of these fields via the JSON payload, including `approved`, `role`, `tier`, and `balance`.
The `authorization` header (containing Bearer tokens) and the raw request body are logged in plaintext via `logger.warning()`. This exposes sensitive authentication credentials in log files.
The endpoint logs the full request body AND the Authorization header (bearer token) to the application logs. This exposes sensitive authentication credentials and request data in plaintext.
User-controlled input is hashed using MD5, which is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks. MD5 should not be used for any security-sensitive purpose.
The endpoint uses MD5 (via `hashlib.md5`) to hash user-supplied data. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.
The ticket_digest_fold_286 endpoint uses MD5, a cryptographically broken hash algorithm, to hash user-supplied phrases.

The `card` query parameter is rendered in a Jinja2 template using the `|safe` filter, which disables HTML escaping. User-controlled content is rendered as raw HTML in the response, leading to Cross-Site Scripting.
The user-controlled `card` parameter is rendered into an HTML response using Jinja2's `|safe` filter which disables auto-escaping, allowing arbitrary HTML/JavaScript injection.
Hardcoded secrets '4812' and '5930' are used to verify user handles 'north' and 'south'. These secrets are embedded in source code and cannot be rotated without code changes.

Authentication/verifier secrets are hardcoded in the source code (`"north": "4812", "south": "5930"`). These secrets are visible to anyone with access to the codebase and cannot be rotated without code changes.
The ticket_identity_hint_659 endpoint returns different error messages for unknown handles ('unknown handle') vs bad verifiers ('bad verifier'), allowing attackers to enumerate valid handles.
The endpoint explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` (disabling browser XSS filter) and empty `Content-Security-Policy` header, weakening browser security protections.
The endpoint explicitly disables XSS-Protection (setting it to '0') and sets CSP to an empty string, removing all content security policy protections.

The `fragment` query parameter is concatenated directly into the Jinja2 template string before rendering. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary Jinja2 template expressions, potentially leading to RCE via accessing Python built-in classes.
The `fragment` parameter from user request is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows SSTI which can lead to remote code execution.
The endpoint determines access level based on the `ops_badge` cookie or `x-ops-badge` header, which are user-controlled inputs. Setting the value to 'lead' grants elevated access with sensitive data.

Authorization is based solely on a trivial cookie or header value (`ops_badge` or `x-ops-badge`) being equal to `"lead"`. An attacker can trivially bypass authorization by setting either of these values.

The `host` query parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `os.system()`. An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands via shell metacharacters (backticks, $(), ;, |, etc.) in the host parameter.

The `host` parameter is directly concatenated into an `os.system()` shell command without any sanitization. An attacker can execute arbitrary OS commands by providing input like `; rm -rf /` or `127.0.0.1 && whoami`.
The `random` module (Mersenne Twister) is used to generate codes instead of `secrets` module. The `random` module is predictable and not suitable for security-sensitive random generation.
Python's `random` module (Mersenne Twister) is used to generate 'nonce' codes. This is not cryptographically secure — an attacker who observes a few nonces can predict future ones.
The `name` query parameter is used directly to construct a file path without sanitization. An attacker can include '../' sequences to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem.
The endpoint uses `ssl._create_unverified_context()` which disables TLS certificate verification, making the connection vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

The endpoint explicitly creates an unverified SSL context (`ssl._create_unverified_context()`) and uses it to make an HTTPS request, disabling certificate validation. This allows man-in-the-middle attacks.

The XML parser is configured with `load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True`, and `no_network=False`, enabling XXE attacks. An attacker can send XML with external entities to read local files, perform SSRF, or cause denial of service.

The project includes `httpx==0.26.0` as a dependency. If httpx is used with default settings, SSL verification is enabled. However, the presence alongside the unverified context usage in support_operations.py suggests inconsistent SSL practices.

The Uvicorn server is started with `reload=True`, which enables auto-reloading on code changes. This is a development feature that should not be enabled in production as it can leak source code and restart the server unexpectedly.

The `packet_ref` query parameter is used directly in constructing a file path via `incoming_dir / packet_ref`. An attacker can use `../` sequences to write files outside the intended directory, potentially overwriting critical system files or writing malicious content.

The `ticket_agent_file_120` endpoint has no authentication gate (`_wrk_gate` dependency is not applied). It returns sensitive operational information including 'renewal risk, payment flags, owner contact details' to any unauthenticated caller.

The `lane` query parameter is used directly as the redirect target in `RedirectResponse()` without any validation. An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs, enabling phishing attacks.

The endpoint logs the full `authorization` header from the incoming request. Authorization headers typically contain Bearer tokens or credentials that should never be logged, as they can be exposed in log files.
The endpoint uses MD5 for hashing user-provided phrases. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks. It should not be used for any security-sensitive purpose.

The `card` query parameter is rendered in a Jinja2 template using the `|safe` filter, which marks the content as safe HTML and prevents auto-escaping. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript by providing a malicious card value.

The `ticket_identity_hint_659` endpoint uses hardcoded handle/verifier pairs (`north: 4812`, `south: 5930`) embedded directly in source code for authentication. These static credentials cannot be rotated without code changes and are visible to anyone with access to the codebase.

The endpoint explicitly sets `X-XSS-Protection: 0` (disabling browser XSS filters) and `Content-Security-Policy: ""` (setting an empty policy that does not restrict any resources). This weakens browser security protections.

The `fragment` query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string without any sanitization. An attacker can execute arbitrary Jinja2 template expressions, leading to server-side template injection (e.g., `{{ config }}`, `{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[2].__subclasses__() }}`) which can lead to remote code execution.

The `ticket_badge_gate_689` endpoint makes an authorization decision based on the `ops_badge` cookie value. Cookies are fully controlled by the client, so any attacker can set `ops_badge=lead` to access elevated data including payroll and casework details.

The `host` query parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `os.system()` without any sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands by providing a host value like `127.0.0.1; id` or `$(cat /etc/passwd)`.

The endpoint uses Python's `random` module (Mersenne Twister) for generating cryptographic tokens. The `random` module is not cryptographically secure and its outputs can be predicted if an attacker can observe a sufficient number of outputs.
The `name` query parameter is used directly in constructing a file path via `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name`. An attacker can use `../` sequences to write files outside the intended directory.
The endpoint uses `ssl._create_unverified_context()` to make an HTTPS request without verifying the server's SSL certificate. This makes the connection vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

The lxml XML parser is configured with `load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True`, and `no_network=False`, which enables external entity processing. An attacker can submit XML with external entities to read local files, perform SSRF, or cause denial of service (e.g., Billion Laughs attack).

The createWebhook call passes the entire whForm object directly to the API, which includes user-controlled 'url' and 'events' fields. If the backend uses object.update() or similar, additional fields could be injected.
The login page hardcodes demo account credentials (email/password pairs) directly in the source code visible to all users.
